text.p: These are the leading stories in the Pakistani press on Sunday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- Foreign donors may halt millions of dollars in vital development aid to war-torn Afghanistan if Kabul's Taleban rulers refuse to allow women back to work and school, a United Nations official said.
- Supporters of Murtaza Bhutto, the slain brother of Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto, have requested President Farooq Leghari to head an inquiry into his death.
- U.S. Assistant Secretary of State Robin Raphel said Pakistan was reluctant to hold a dialogue with India on the disputed northern state of Kashmir.
- A heavy downpour on Saturday morning in the entire cotton belt of Punjab province has minimised the danger of pest attack.
- Arrival of seed cotton gained momentum as 863,000 375-lb bales reached ginning factories by October 1 compared to none in the same period last year.
- Morocco's Office Cherifen des Phosphate (OCP), the world's main exporter of phosphates and by-products, has signed a $220 million deal with Pakistan to set up a fertiliser plant in Karachi.

- All staff of the state-run Pakistan Telecommunication Ltd (PTCL) plan to stage a nationwide strike on October 7. The PTCL management has warned employees that they risk disciplinary action if they go ahead with the action.
- The government will review on Tuesday progress on all the memoranda of understanding signed by Pakistan with foreign investors during the last 30 months, sources said.
- The government plans to import 1.8 million tonnes of wheat by May 1997, State Minister for Food Ayub Jattak said.
- Taleban religious militia launched an offensive against the forces of ousted president Burhanuddin Rabbani in the Panjshir Valley, witnesses said.
- Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto said Pakistan had no involvement with the Taleban in Afghanistan and called for a better understanding with Russia on the issue.

- The International Finance Corporation, the World Bank's private lending arm, said Pakistan's macro-economic situation had begun to improve in 1996 after the government initiated a major adjustment programme in response to a near-crisis in November 1995.
- The customs authorities have issued several hundred notices telling importers that clearance of their consignments had been stopped pending payment of outstanding dues.
